title: Projectile motion and admissible flight times
objective: Model a projectile with vector initial conditions, select physically admissible roots, and explain the limits of the constant-gravity approximation.
why: A quadratic can give two mathematically valid event times, yet only one may describe a future landing. Projectile motion brings together components, calculus, roots, and model restrictions. You will predict a complete flight, check its highest point and landing state, and explain why a familiar formula can fail when its assumptions change.

prerequisites.label: Motion and relative velocity in three dimensions

sections.heading: Declare the ideal flight model
paragraphs: A projectile is an object moving after launch under the forces included in a stated model. Here it is a point object acted on only by a constant downward gravitational acceleration. We neglect air resistance, wind forces, buoyancy, and rotation effects. The ground is a flat plane, and the trajectory ends when it contacts the specified landing surface.

Choose +x horizontally and +y upward, with the ground at y=0. Let initial height be h≥0 and initial velocity components be vₓ₀ and vᵧ₀. Define g as a positive magnitude, so $a_x=0$ and $a_y=-g$. A negative vertical acceleration is not a negative value of the magnitude g.

Near Earth's surface a value around 9.81 m/s² is often a useful approximation for g, but the appropriate value depends on location and required accuracy. Worked examples and generated questions here explicitly use g=10 m/s² to make exact calculations transparent. The investigation lets you change g; its entered value is a model input, not a measured planetary constant.

The constant-gravity approximation assumes the flight region is small enough that changes in gravitational magnitude and direction can be neglected. Flat-ground and no-drag assumptions also need justification for an intended application. A clean parabola is a consequence of these assumptions, not a guarantee about every thrown or launched object.

sections.heading: Derive the component equations from acceleration
paragraphs: Integrating the constant acceleration gives $v_x(t)=v_{x0}$ and $v_y(t)=v_{y0}-gt$. Integrating again, with x(0)=0 and y(0)=h, gives $x(t)=v_{x0}t$ and $y(t)=h+v_{y0}t-gt^2/2$. All components describe the same event time t.

The vertical equation has no horizontal velocity in it. Thus two ideal launches with the same h, vᵧ₀, and g have identical vertical motion and landing time even if their horizontal velocities differ. Their horizontal positions differ. This independence depends on the force model; speed-dependent drag can couple the components.

If vₓ₀≠0, eliminating t yields $y=h+(v_{y0}/v_{x0})x-gx^2/(2v_{x0}^2)$, a parabola in these coordinates. The equation alone is not the full physical flight: restrict x to the positions reached during the admissible time interval. If vₓ₀=0, do not divide by it; the flight is vertical with x fixed at zero.

The horizontal displacement to landing is Δx=vₓ₀T. It can be negative if the launch is toward negative x. Its magnitude is horizontal travel distance, not total length along the curved flight path. We ask for signed horizontal displacement unless a question explicitly requests a nonnegative range.

sections.heading: Resolve a launch angle without changing conventions
paragraphs: For a launch speed v₀ and angle theta measured from +x toward +y, $v_{x0}=v_0\cos\theta$ and $v_{y0}=v_0\sin\theta$. State the angular unit and use a matching calculator mode. If an angle is instead measured from the vertical, the component formulas change because the adjacent and opposite sides change.

At 30 degrees above +x, cos(theta)=sqrt(3)/2 and sin(theta)=1/2. A 20 m/s launch therefore has components (10sqrt(3),10) m/s. Squaring and adding checks that the magnitude remains 20 m/s. Assigning both components the full speed would create a different launch with a larger total speed.

An angle greater than 90 degrees can give negative horizontal velocity while the projectile still rises initially. Component signs determine the direction. In many engineering problems it is clearer to give the signed components directly, as the investigation does, than to rely on an unstated angle convention.

Keep exact fractions and square roots in exact-answer questions. Approximate comparison questions state their units and tolerances. Rounding a flight time before multiplying by horizontal velocity can create avoidable displacement error, so retain extra precision until the requested final value.

sections.heading: Solve the landing equation and enforce the event definition
paragraphs: For ground impact, set y(T)=0. The quadratic formula gives $T=[v_{y0}\pm\sqrt{v_{y0}^2+2gh}]/g$. When h>0 and g>0, the square root is larger than |vᵧ₀|, so one root is positive and the other is negative. Select the positive root for a launch beginning at t=0; the negative root belongs to a backward mathematical extension.

If h=0 and vᵧ₀>0, the roots are 0 and 2vᵧ₀/g. The first is the departure event, while the second is the later return to the ground. A question about flight duration after departure needs the positive return time. A question asking for every algebraic root needs both values.

If h=0 and vᵧ₀≤0, no positive airborne interval begins under this ground-boundary model. The free-flight formula would immediately put the object below the ground. Report zero airborne duration and stop; a contact, rolling, or bounce model is needed to describe subsequent motion. Do not convert a negative root into a negative elapsed duration.

For a landing surface at a different height H, solve h+vᵧ₀T-gT²/2=H instead. A level above the highest attainable point has no real crossing. A lower reference height can have two crossings, one ascending and one descending, if both lie within the flight. Specify whether it is a reference level or a physical obstacle that ends motion at its first collision.

After selecting a candidate time, substitute it into the original vertical equation, verify that it belongs to the modeled interval, and evaluate all other coordinates at that same time. Algebraic correctness and physical admissibility are separate checks.

sections.heading: The highest point does not switch gravity off
paragraphs: For an initially upward launch, the highest point occurs when vᵧ=0, at $t_{\mathrm{top}}=v_{y0}/g$. Substituting gives $y_{\mathrm{max}}=h+v_{y0}^2/(2g)$. The vertical velocity changes from positive to negative there, while the downward acceleration remains -g.

At the top the velocity vector is (vₓ₀,0). Its speed is |vₓ₀|, which is nonzero for an oblique launch. Only a purely vertical launch has the entire velocity vector equal to zero at its top in this model. Even then the acceleration is nonzero and the object starts descending immediately afterward.

For vᵧ₀≤0, the initial point is already the highest point during the future flight. Solving vᵧ₀-gt=0 may give a time at or before launch; a negative time is not a future apex. The maximum on a restricted interval can occur at an endpoint rather than at an interior derivative zero.

Ascent and descent times are equal only between equal heights under this ideal model. A projectile launched above the ground spends extra time descending below its launch height. Doubling the time to the top does not give ground-impact time when the landing height differs from the launch height.

sections.heading: A 45-degree range rule has specific conditions
paragraphs: For equal launch and landing heights with upward launch and positive horizontal motion, flight time is T=2v₀sin(theta)/g. Multiplying by v₀cos(theta) and using the double-angle identity gives $R=v_0^2\sin(2\theta)/g$. With fixed launch speed, no drag, constant g, and equal heights, this horizontal range is largest at theta=45 degrees.

If the landing height changes, derive T from the vertical equation before multiplying by horizontal velocity. In particular, a launch from above the landing surface gains descent time that the same-height formula omits. The angle that maximizes range can differ from 45 degrees. Comparing two selected angles is also different from optimizing over every possible angle.

Constraints on landing direction, obstacles, or allowable flight time can change what an engineering design should maximize. A largest horizontal displacement is not automatically a suitable trajectory. Here we isolate the mathematical range comparison and identify its assumptions; later projects will require an explicit purpose and evidence for model choices.

When using a plot with different horizontal and vertical scales, the visible angle of its curve is not the physical launch angle. Recover that angle from the velocity components, with quadrant awareness. The investigation labels its separate axis scales and supplies the coordinate table so a drawing does not become hidden numerical evidence.

sections.heading: Inspect the landing velocity and the model's end
paragraphs: At an admissible impact time T, velocity just before contact is $(v_{x0},v_{y0}-gT)$. Its magnitude is the impact speed. Do not use the average flight velocity in place of this instantaneous vector. A negative y component means downward motion in the chosen axes.

The vertical constant-acceleration identity offers an independent check: $v_y^2=v_{y0}^2-2g(y-h)$. At ground impact it gives vᵧ²=vᵧ₀²+2gh. It checks speed magnitude but loses the sign; the descending time history selects the negative vertical velocity just before impact.

The ideal equations describe only the interval ending at contact. They do not determine rebound, deformation, or stopping time. Those require information about forces and material behavior. A trajectory drawn through the ground would be an extrapolation outside the model, not a prediction of the collision.

A real flight's disagreement with the ideal model can indicate drag, wind, uncertain launch conditions, measurement error, or an unsuitable gravitational or surface approximation. Distinguish these possibilities with observations and a revised model. Resource links or a smoothly rendered curve are not experimental validation.

examples.title: Select the future landing from two roots
examples.prompt: Use the ideal no-drag model with g=10 m/s². A projectile starts 10 m above the ground with velocity (6,5) m/s. Find ground-impact time, horizontal displacement, and velocity just before contact.

steps.reason: Integrate the component accelerations (0,-10) using the supplied initial state.
Both values satisfy the quadratic, but only 2 s follows the launch at zero.
Evaluate both position and velocity at the same admissible impact time.
The vertical squared-velocity identity checks the impact magnitude. The descending trajectory selects v_y=-15 rather than +15.

examples.conclusion: The flight lasts 2 s and ends 12 m along +x. Just before contact velocity is (6,-15) m/s. The -1 s root is a backward extension, not a future landing.

examples.title: A horizontal launch begins at its highest point
examples.prompt: An ideal projectile starts at height 20 m with velocity (8,0) m/s and g=10 m/s². Find flight time and horizontal displacement, then describe vertical motion at launch.

steps.reason: The initial vertical velocity is zero, but acceleration is not. Choose the positive root for future impact.
Horizontal motion accumulates at constant 8 m/s during the same two-second interval.
Immediately after launch the vertical velocity is negative. There is no later upward portion or future interior apex.

examples.conclusion: Flight time is 2 s and horizontal displacement is 16 m. The initial height is the maximum; zero initial vertical velocity does not imply zero vertical acceleration.

examples.title: Resolve an angle and check the same-height formulas
examples.prompt: An ideal projectile launches from ground level at 20 m/s, 30 degrees above +x, with g=10 m/s². Find its components, later return time, horizontal displacement, and maximum height.

steps.reason: The angle is measured from the horizontal. The component squares sum to 400, recovering the stated speed.
The zero-time root is launch. The positive root is the later return to the same height.
Horizontal speed stays constant and the vertical velocity vanishes after one second.
The vertical velocity-time triangle gives the height gain. Horizontal motion remains at the apex.

examples.conclusion: The exact horizontal displacement is 20sqrt(3) m and the peak height is 5 m. The whole velocity vector is not zero at the top.

examples.title: Distinguish crossings, an apex touch, and an unreachable height
examples.prompt: A projectile starts at height 5 m with vertical velocity 20 m/s and g=10 m/s². The target levels are reference heights, not physical barriers. Find times at heights 20, 25, and 30 m.

steps.reason: Completing the square exposes the maximum height of 25 m at 2 s.
The lower level is crossed on ascent and descent. Both times are positive and occur before ground contact.
A repeated algebraic root represents one distinct event time at the apex.
There is no real time at that height. A complex number is not a physical event time in this model.

examples.conclusion: Height 20 m occurs at 1 and 3 s, height 25 m only at 2 s, and height 30 m is unreachable. A physical obstacle would require checking which crossing causes the first actual collision.

examples.title: Compare angles when launch and landing heights differ
examples.prompt: An ideal projectile launches from height 80 m at speed 20 m/s with g=10 m/s². Compare horizontal displacements for 30-degree and 45-degree launches above +x.

steps.reason: Resolve the speed into components before calculating the landing time.
The positive quadratic root includes the extra descent from the raised launch.
Multiply the horizontal component by that angle's flight time.
The 45-degree launch has a longer flight but a smaller horizontal component; both changes matter.

examples.conclusion: Of these two launches, 30 degrees goes farther. This is not a claim that 30 degrees is the optimum among all angles. The familiar 45-degree rule required equal launch and landing heights.

examples.title: A downward boundary launch has no airborne interval
examples.prompt: A point object starts at ground level with velocity (4,-2) m/s. The ideal free-flight model uses g=10 m/s² and ends at ground contact. Determine its future airborne duration.

steps.reason: For any positive time, both factors on the final right side make y negative.
Zero is the current boundary event; the other root is in the past.
No positive time interval satisfies the free-flight domain above the ground. Continuing requires different contact physics.

examples.conclusion: The modeled airborne duration is zero. Neither a negative duration nor a trajectory continued below the ground is an admissible free flight.

guided.title: Reject the past root and retain the velocity direction
guided.setup: An ideal projectile starts at height 15 m with velocity (-4,10) m/s. Use +y upward, ground at y=0, no drag, and g=10 m/s².
before: The algebraic ground-crossing times are 3 s and -1 s. Choose the future landing for launch at t=0.
Horizontal position is -4t and vertical velocity is 10-10t. Evaluate both at the selected landing time.

question.prompt: Find the future flight time, signed horizontal displacement, and vertical velocity just before impact. Then identify what happens at the highest point.

options.label: The entire velocity and acceleration are zero
options.feedback: Only vertical velocity is zero at the top of this oblique flight. The horizontal velocity is -4 m/s and vertical acceleration is -10 m/s².

options.label: Velocity is (-4,0) m/s and acceleration remains (0,-10) m/s²
options.feedback: Horizontal velocity is constant, while vertical velocity changes sign under persistent downward acceleration.

options.label: Gravity is temporarily absent, then returns on descent
options.feedback: Gravity does not switch off at the apex. The unchanged downward acceleration causes the vertical velocity to pass through zero.

hints: Use T=3 s; the -1 s root lies before the modeled launch.
Horizontal displacement is (-4)(3)=-12 m. The negative sign records motion toward negative x.
Vertical impact velocity is 10-10(3)=-20 m/s. At the top only the vertical velocity vanishes.
explanation: The future landing is at 3 s, where 15+10(3)-5(3)²=0. Horizontal displacement is -12 m and the vertical impact velocity is -20 m/s.
The apex occurs at 1 s. Its velocity is (-4,0) m/s, while acceleration remains (0,-10) m/s². The speed there is 4 m/s, not zero.
question.answerSummary: T=3 s; horizontal displacement -12 m; vertical impact velocity -20 m/s; horizontal motion and gravity persist at the top.

guided.after: Check the impact magnitude independently: v_y²=10²+2(10)(15)=400 m²/s². The descending branch selects -20 m/s. Taking a positive square root would lose the physical direction.

interaction.prompt: Predict the flight time, signed horizontal displacement, maximum height, and vertical impact velocity. Inspect the trajectory and table, then vary one launch component at a time and test the limits of the flight model.

summary: Declare the axes, initial height and velocity, positive magnitude g, force assumptions, landing surface, and modeled time interval.
Constant downward gravity without drag gives constant horizontal velocity and vertical velocity vᵧ₀-gt. Both components share the same time.
Resolve launch speed using the stated angle convention, and check the component norm.
Find algebraic event roots, then enforce the physical domain. A launch at ground level can have both a departure root and a later return root.
At an upward flight's apex, vertical velocity is zero but downward acceleration remains. Horizontal velocity generally remains nonzero.
Target heights can have two crossings, one apex touch, or no real event. A reference level and a collision surface are different models.
The 45-degree range optimum assumes fixed speed, equal heights, constant gravity, no drag, and an unconstrained ideal flight.
Stop the free-flight model at contact. Check landing velocity with both its time law and the squared-velocity identity, retaining the physical sign.
retrieval: An ideal projectile starts at height 20 m with velocity (3,0) m/s and g=10 m/s². Find flight time, horizontal displacement, highest point, and impact velocity. Then double only the horizontal component. Check after working: T=2 s, displacement 6 m, highest height 20 m at launch, and impact velocity (3,-20) m/s. Doubling the horizontal component doubles displacement and that velocity component while leaving the flight time and vertical motion unchanged.
